Calibration is fitting a model's parameters to data: finding the values for which the model's results match what was observed. A model of a measles outbreak may know from the literature how long people are infectious, but not how fast measles spreads in this particular town, or what share of cases were reported: those are the parameters to estimate. A best fit (the single set of values that fits best) is usually enough for a first exploration; when the uncertainty in the values matters too, a posterior (the distribution of values consistent with the data) can be fitted instead.

In Starsim, calibration needs two things: **which parameters are unknown**, as parameters with `bounds` (`ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4])`), and **the data**, attached to the sim in columns named like the results they measure. `sim.fit()` then fits every parameter that has bounds to every result that has data, with no function to write that puts values into the model or pulls results out.

The [calibration tutorial](../tutorials/t6_data.qmd) goes through one fit step by step. [Fitting methods](calibration_methods.qmd) compares the methods, [Fit diagnostics](calibration_diagnostics.qmd) covers what to check afterwards, [Gradients](calibration_gradients.qmd) covers posteriors and profile likelihoods of ODEs, and [Optimization](calibration_optimization.qmd) uses the same machinery to allocate a budget.

## A first fit

The model is a measles outbreak in a town of 100,000 people, 90% of whom are immune, using the library's measles model, `ssl.Measles` (S to E to I to R). The latent and infectious periods are exponential here, which keeps each fit quick. Reported cases, `report` times the onsets, are added to the library's model as an outcome. Three things are unknown: the transmission rate `beta`, the share reported `report`, and the share infectious at the start, `I0`:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import starsim as ss
import starsim.library as ssl

beta   = ss.par(1.0, bounds=[0.3, 3])        # Transmission rate per day: unknown
report = ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.05, 1])       # Share of cases reported: unknown
I0     = ss.par(0.0001, bounds=[1e-5, 1e-3]) # Share infectious at the start (10 people): unknown

cases = ss.outcome(report*ssl.Measles.onset) # Reported cases: a share of the onsets, added to the library's model
measles = ssl.Measles(beta=beta, dur_exp=ss.expon(ss.days(8)), dur_inf=ss.expon(ss.days(11)), cases=cases, init=dict(I=I0, R=0.9))

pars = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')
```

## R

```r
library(starsim) # Also gives ssl, Starsim's library, as in Python's import starsim.library as ssl

beta   <- par(1.0, bounds = c(0.3, 3), name = "beta")      # Transmission rate per day: unknown
report <- par(0.3, bounds = c(0.05, 1), name = "report")   # Share of cases reported: unknown
I0     <- par(0.0001, bounds = c(1e-5, 1e-3), name = "I0") # Share infectious at the start (10 people): unknown

cases <- outcome(report * ssl$Measles$onset) # Reported cases: a share of the onsets, added to the library's model
measles <- ssl$Measles(beta = beta, dur_exp = ss$expon(days(8)), dur_inf = ss$expon(days(11)), cases = cases, init = list(I = I0, R = 0.9))

make_sim <- function(...) { # A sim with these settings, and any others given
  Sim(measles, total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2026-01-01", ...)
}
```
:::

The value given to each parameter is where the search starts, and the bounds are the range it searches. A parameter is named by its variable (`I0` here), or by `name=`.

The data here are weekly reported cases made from an agent-based run of the same disease, with `beta = 1.4`, half of cases reported, 30 people infectious at the start, and counts that vary more than Poisson counts. Real data would be read from a file instead (see [below](#the-data)):

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
truth = ss.Sim(measles, pars=dict(beta=1.4, report=0.5, I0=0.0003), n_agents=100_000, rand_seed=3, verbose=0, **pars)
truth.run()
data = truth.to_synthetic_data('cases', resample='week', noise=ss.nbinom(n=10)) # Weekly cases (whole weeks only, so not the last, partial one), with more variation than Poisson counts
data.head()
```

## R

```r
truth <- make_sim(pars = list(beta = 1.4, report = 0.5, I0 = 0.0003), n_agents = 100000, rand_seed = 3, verbose = 0)
truth$run()
data <- truth$to_synthetic_data("cases", resample = "week", noise = ss$nbinom(n = 10)) # Weekly cases (whole weeks only, so not the last, partial one), with more variation than Poisson counts, as a data frame
head(data)
```
:::

Attach the data to a sim of the model, and fit:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(measles, data=data, **pars)
fit = sim.fit(method='nelder-mead')
```

## R

```r
sim <- make_sim(data = data)
fit <- sim$fit(method = "nelder-mead")
```
:::

By default an ODE with three parameters is fitted by gradients (`'l-bfgs-b'`); Nelder-Mead is quicker for a model this small. The fit prints whether it converged, and (if not given a method) which method it chose and why. `fit.summarize()` shows the values found, with the loss before and after:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
fit.summarize()
```

## R

```r
fit$summarize() # Prints the values found
```
:::

A fitted initial condition is where the model has to start to match the data, not a count of who was infectious on day one. `fit.plot()` shows the model, summed over each week of the data, before and after the fit:

```{python}
fit.plot()
```

The original sim is not changed. The fit holds the best values (`fit.pars`, which can be passed to `ss.Sim(pars=...)`), the calibrated sim (`fit.sim`, already run), and the sim with the starting values (`fit.before`); everything else it holds is in the [appendix](#what-a-fit-holds).

```{python}
fit.pars
```

## Parameters and data

Every parameter with `bounds` is fitted, wherever it is: a rate, a share, a duration (with bounds in its own unit, e.g. `ss.par(ss.days(8), bounds=[5, 12])`), an initial condition, a parameter of a network or intervention, a value for each level of a stratification, an array, a time series, or a setting of the sim. Each kind, and how it is named in `fit.pars`, is in the [appendix](#what-can-be-fitted). In addition:

- `pars=` fits only the parameters named, keeping the others at their values: `sim.fit(pars=['beta'])`.
- Wide positive bounds (the high end 10 or more times the low end) are searched on a log scale, since going from 0.01 to 0.02 doubles transmission, but going from 0.11 to 0.12 hardly changes it. The fit says which.
- A prior, `ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4], prior=ss.normal(2, 0.3))`, is used by the methods that use likelihoods; without one, the prior is uniform over the bounds.
- `penalty=` adds a function of the values to what a best fit minimizes, e.g. to keep a curve smooth: `sim.fit(penalty=lambda pars: 10*np.sum(np.diff(pars['curve'], 2)**2))`.

### A value that isn't a parameter

A value set in code, such as a setting of an intervention that its constructor doesn't take, is fitted by writing a function that sets it, with the value as a keyword argument given as `ss.par`, and giving the function as a module (a function given as an intervention is called at every step):

```python
def set_testing(sim, symp_prob=ss.par(0.1, bounds=[0.01, 0.5])):
    sim.interventions.testing.symp_prob = symp_prob
    sim.interventions.testing.asymp_prob = symp_prob/10

sim = ss.Sim(..., interventions=[set_testing, testing], data=data)
fit = sim.fit() # Fits symp_prob, with the others
```

The value is then a parameter like any other: `fit.pars.symp_prob`, `ss.Sim(pars=dict(symp_prob=0.2))`, `sim.sensitivity()`, and `ss.parallel(sim, pars=dict(symp_prob=[0.1, 0.2]))` all find it by name.

### The data

The data have a time column (`date`, `year`, `t`, or `time`; an integer `year` is a calendar year), or dates as the index, and one column for each data series, named like the result it is compared with, here `cases`. A column that could match results of more than one module is named with the module, e.g. `measles.cases`. Any result can have data, including an analyzer's (`by_age.cancers_0_15`), a nested one (`hpv.genotype.cancers`), or a column of a result (`sis.infection.alpha`).

The data need not be on the model's time step, since each result knows what kind of quantity it is:

- A **flow**, like reported cases, is summed over each interval of the data, from its date to the next: each week is dated by its first day. Data dated by the end of each period ("week ending") need their dates moved back by one period first, e.g. `data['date'] -= pd.Timedelta(days=7)`; Starsim warns if the last row starts a period that ends after the run, as end-labeled data often does.
- A **stock** (like the number infectious) or a **ratio** (like prevalence) is compared with the model's value at the data's time.
- Data by calendar year are compared over the year: a flow summed, and a stock or ratio averaged.

`data=` takes a dataframe or a file name. `ss.SimData()` renames columns on the way in, and can ignore the rest:

```python
data = ss.SimData('town_cases.csv', aliases=dict(cases='Reported cases (weekly)', date='Week starting'), ignore_extra=True)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, data=data, **pars)
```

A column that matches no result gets a note listing the closest result names when the sim is initialized, and is an error when fitted. `weights=` weighs series differently, e.g. `sim.fit(weights=dict(cases=1, deaths=5))`; in a posterior, a weight of 5 counts the data five times over and makes the posterior too narrow, so use weights for best fits.

### Which parameters matter

A parameter that the results don't depend on can't be fitted. `sim.sensitivity()` needs no data: it samples the parameters over their bounds, runs the model at each, and gives the partial rank correlation of each parameter with a summary of each result (near 1 or -1, the result moves with the parameter; near 0, it doesn't):

```{python}
sens = sim.sensitivity(n=50, verbose=False)
sens[['measles.I peak', 'measles.cases total']]
```

## Measuring the fit

Without a likelihood, the measure of fit is the **normalized absolute error**: for each data series, the mean absolute difference between model and data, divided by the mean of the data, which puts series of different sizes on one scale. `loss='rmse'` uses the root mean squared error instead, and `loss=` can be a function of the sim that returns the mismatch to minimize:

```python
def peak_error(sim):
    """ How far the model's peak week is from the observed peak, in weeks """
    weekly = sim.results.measles.cases.resample('week')
    return abs(weekly.values.argmax() - data.cases.values.argmax())

fit = sim.fit(loss=peak_error)
```

A **likelihood** says how the data vary around the model's value, which is the mean. It can be declared on the outcome, for every fit, or given to the fit:

```python
cases = ss.outcome(report*ssl.Measles.onset, likelihood=ss.poisson()) # On the outcome
fit = sim.fit(likelihood=dict(cases=ss.nbinom(n=10)))     # Or for one fit, by series
fit = sim.fit(likelihood=ss.nbinom(n=10))                  # Or the same for every series
```

The likelihoods are listed in the [appendix](#likelihoods-and-priors). A likelihood can also be a function `fn(observed, model)` that returns the log-likelihood of each value; it can't be differentiated in JAX, so the default fit then uses Nelder-Mead.

With a likelihood for every series, the fit maximizes their summed log-likelihood (for a stochastic model, an estimate of it; see [below](#a-stochastic-model)), and the methods that give a posterior can be used. A fit uses likelihoods for every series or for none: a mix, or likelihoods with `loss=`, is an error. A negative binomial suits reported cases, and its dispersion `n` (smaller is more variable) can be fitted too:

```{python}
dispersion = ss.par(5, bounds=[1, 100], name='dispersion')
fit_lik = sim.fit(method='nelder-mead', likelihood=dict(cases=ss.nbinom(n=dispersion)), verbose=False)
fit_lik.table
```

To score any run that has data, e.g. to compare scenarios, `ss.fitting.mismatch(sim)` gives the normalized absolute error (or another `loss=`) and `ss.fitting.loglik(sim, likelihood=...)` the log-likelihood (with `by_series=True`, for each series; with `data=`, against other data):

```{python}
print('Normalized absolute error:', ss.fitting.mismatch(fit_lik.sim))
print('Log-likelihood:', ss.fitting.loglik(fit_lik.sim, likelihood=dict(cases=ss.nbinom(n=fit_lik.pars.dispersion))))
```

## How the fit is found

By default a fit is a best fit, by a method that suits the model, which `sim.fit()` prints with its reason. A posterior is always asked for by name:

| The model | The default method (a best fit) | A posterior, by name |
|---|---|---|
| Deterministic (an ODE) | `'l-bfgs-b'` (gradients from JAX, or by finite differences); `'nelder-mead'` for one or two parameters, or when JAX can't take the log-likelihood | `'nuts'`, given a likelihood for every series; `'pmcmc'` if JAX can't run the model |
| Stochastic compartmental | `'optuna'` | `'pmcmc'` (particle MCMC), given a likelihood for every series |
| Agent-based | `'optuna'` | `'abc-smc'`, which needs no likelihood |

`'powell'`, `'slsqp'`, and `'if2'` can also be named; [Fitting methods](calibration_methods.qmd) compares them all. A method's settings are given with it: `method=ss.fitting.method('nuts', draws=1000, chains=2)`, and a setting the method does not take is an error. A list, such as `method=['optuna', 'nelder-mead']`, runs each method in turn from the best values of the one before.

### A stochastic model

A stochastic model gives a different result on each run, so each set of values gets a noisy score. Starsim fits it with [Optuna](https://optuna.org), which tries values, scores them by running the model, and uses the scores to choose where to try next. Here is the same model as a chain binomial:

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(measles, data=data, solver='binomial', **pars)
fit = sim.fit(method='optuna', rand_seed=5)
fit.summarize()
```

The search can settle anywhere in a region of similar scores (`spread_lower` to `spread_upper`, the range of the best tenth of the trials). The settings that matter most are `n_trials=` and `n_runs=` (the runs that score each trial), given as `ss.fitting.method('optuna', n_trials=500)`; all are listed in [Fitting methods](calibration_methods.qmd#appendix-settings-of-each-method). `rand_seed=` of `sim.fit()` makes the fit reproducible. Agents are fitted the same way, usually with more trials.

`ss.Transition(..., noise=sigma)` adds gamma white noise to a transition's rate, for models whose rates vary at random from day to day; the particle filter, IF2, and particle MCMC all see it (see [Measles in London](../gallery/measles_london.qmd#declared-with-noise)).

`fit.sim` is one run with the best values; for a stochastic model, compare the data with many:

```{python}
msim = ss.parallel(fit.sim, n_runs=20)
```

```{python}
msim.plot('measles.cases')
```

## Using the fit

The calibrated sim is the starting point for scenarios: `sim.new()` makes a new sim from the same inputs, with whatever is given changed, and from `fit.sim` that includes the fitted values. Here, a catch-up campaign on 1 April that vaccinates half of those still susceptible, compared with none:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
vaccination = ss.vaccinate(efficacy=0.97, who=measles.S, when='2025-04-01', coverage=0.5)
scenarios = {
    'No campaign': fit.sim.new(),
    'Campaign':    fit.sim.new(interventions=vaccination),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios, n_runs=20)
msim.plot('measles.cases')
```

## R

```r
vaccination <- vaccinate(efficacy = 0.97, who = measles$S, when = "2025-04-01", coverage = 0.5)
scenarios <- list(
  "No campaign" = fit$sim$new(),
  "Campaign"    = fit$sim$new(interventions = vaccination)
)
msim <- parallel(scenarios, n_runs = 20)
msim$plot("measles.cases")
```
:::

```{python}
msim.summarize().loc['measles_cases']
```

Strictly speaking, this is not the right thing to do: these runs all use the best values, so their spread is the model's own noise, not uncertainty about the values. `fit.project(scenarios, **kwargs)` runs scenarios from the fit, passing `kwargs` to `sim.new()`, e.g. `fit.project({'No campaign': None, 'Campaign': vaccination}, stop='2026-06-01')` to forecast past the data; from a posterior, the runs carry the uncertainty in the values too ([T6](../tutorials/t6_data.qmd#projecting-from-the-fit) has an example checked against what happened next).

### Projecting from a posterior

`fit.project()` from a posterior runs once for each of `n_runs` draws (100 by default), with the same draws and seeds in every scenario:

- **With `'pmcmc'` or `'abc-smc'` on a stochastic compartmental model**, each draw comes with a run (`fit.trajectories`) that follows the data, and by default the projection continues it from the last data point, so the scenarios differ only after it. Continued runs are kept as results only (`msim.results`).
- **`restart=True`** runs each draw from the start instead, for a scenario that changes something before the last data point. A scenario that can't be continued (e.g. an intervention with a capacity, or a delivery before the last data point) is run from the start with a warning; `restart=False` makes that an error.
- **For an ODE**, a run at the same values is always the same, so the two are the same; see [Gradients](calibration_gradients.qmd#projecting-from-a-posterior).

[Fit diagnostics](calibration_diagnostics.qmd) covers what to check before using a fit: a best value at a bound, parameters the data can't tell apart, a lucky trial, and too few runs to judge.

- [pomp: Getting started](https://kingaa.github.io/pomp/vignettes/getting_started.html): likelihood-based fitting of stochastic models, including iterated filtering, in R

## Appendix

### What can be fitted

Every kind of value that a fit can take as a parameter, and how it is named in `fit.pars` (and so in `pars=`, `ss.Sim(pars=...)`, and `sim.sensitivity()`):

| What | Given as | Named in `fit.pars` |
|---|---|---|
| A rate, share, or duration of a declared model | `beta = ss.par(1.5, bounds=[0.5, 4])`, used in a transition or outcome | By its variable, `beta`, or its `name=`; with the module's name, `measles.beta`, if several modules have one of that name |
| An initial condition | `init=dict(I=ss.par(...))` (a share), or `init_n=dict(I=ss.par(10, bounds=[1, 100], name='I0'))` (a number); without a variable or `name=`, an error | By its variable or `name=`, as `I0` on this page |
| A value for each level of a stratification | `ss.par(ss.by(age=[...]), bounds=...)` | One for each level, by its label, e.g. `beta[0-14]` and `beta[15+]`; whole in `fit.pars` |
| An array | `ss.par(np.array([...]), bounds=[lows, highs])` | `curve[0]`, `curve[1]`, ... (not those whose low and high bounds are equal); whole in `fit.pars` |
| A time series | `ss.par(ss.timeseries(days, values), bounds=...)` | By its times, `beta[0]`, `beta[14]`, ...; whole in `fit.pars` |
| A parameter of a module written as code | `ssl.HIV(beta=ss.par(0.01, bounds=[0.001, 0.1]))` | `beta`, or `hiv.beta` if the name is taken |
| A value in a dict parameter | `cin_fn=dict(k=ss.par(0.3, bounds=[0.1, 0.5]))` | `cin_fn.k` |
| A modifier's amount | `ss.modify(hiv.rel_sus, multiply=ss.par(2.7, bounds=[1, 4]))` | `multiply`, or its name as a parameter of a declared disease |
| A parameter of a network, intervention, or other module | `ss.vaccinate(coverage=ss.par(0.5, bounds=[0.2, 0.9]))` | Its name, e.g. `coverage`, with its module's name if needed |
| A keyword argument of a function given as a module | `def set_testing(sim, symp_prob=ss.par(...))` | `symp_prob` |
| A likelihood's own parameter | `ss.nbinom(n=ss.par(5, bounds=[1, 100], name='dispersion'))` | `dispersion` (fitted only by a fit that uses the likelihood) |
| A setting of the sim | `ss.Sim(n_agents=ss.par(5000, bounds=[1000, 20000]))`, fitted with a new sim for each value | `n_agents` |

### Likelihoods and priors

The likelihoods that `likelihood=` (or `ss.outcome(..., likelihood=)`) takes. In each, the model's value is the mean (or, for a share, the probability). "In JAX" means the log-likelihood can be taken in JAX, as gradient-based fits and NUTS need:

| Likelihood | For data that are | In JAX |
|---|---|---|
| `ss.poisson()` | Counts, such as reported cases | Yes |
| `ss.nbinom(n=...)` | Counts that vary more than a Poisson, with `n` the dispersion (smaller is more variable); `n` can be an `ss.par` with bounds, and is then fitted | Yes |
| `ss.normal(std=...)` | Continuous values, with the standard deviation `std` | Yes |
| `ss.lognormal(std=...)` | Positive continuous values, with the standard deviation `std` | Yes |
| `ss.binom(n=...)` | The number who test positive out of `n` surveyed, with the model's share (e.g. a prevalence) as the probability | Yes |
| `ss.bernoulli()` | Yes or no outcomes | Yes |
| A function `fn(observed, model)` | Anything else (e.g. a beta-binomial from SciPy): it returns the log-likelihood of each value | No: the default fit uses Nelder-Mead; a method with gradients needs `require_jax=False` |

The priors that `ss.par(..., prior=)` takes. Without one, the prior is uniform over the bounds, on the value itself, even for a parameter searched on a log scale; give a parameter whose order of magnitude is uncertain a prior such as `ss.lognormal()`:

| Prior | In JAX |
|---|---|
| `ss.normal()`, `ss.lognormal()`, `ss.gamma()`, `ss.beta_dist()`, `ss.expon()`, `ss.uniform()` | Yes |
| Any other distribution that has a density (e.g. `ss.weibull()`) | No: it works with the methods that run with Python in the loop |

### What a fit holds

The attributes of the `ss.fitting.Fit` that `sim.fit()` returns (see [ss.fitting.Fit](../api/fit.qmd)):

| Attribute | What it is |
|---|---|
| `fit.pars` | The best values, which can be passed to `ss.Sim(pars=...)` |
| `fit.sim` | The calibrated sim: a copy of the original with the best values, already run |
| `fit.before` | The sim with the starting values, already run |
| `fit.table` | Each parameter's starting value, best value, and bounds; with a posterior, also its median, 95% interval (`lower`, `upper`), `rhat`, and `ess`; with Optuna and IF2, `spread_lower` and `spread_upper` (an indication of the uncertainty, not an interval) |
| `fit.method` | The method used |
| `fit.objective`, `fit.objective_before` | The loss (or the negative log-likelihood, or log-posterior) at the best and starting values; for a stochastic model, an estimate; `fit.measure` says which |
| `fit.scores` | The score of the best values in each run; their spread is the run-to-run noise of a stochastic fit |
| `fit.converged`, `fit.why` | Whether the method reached its own stopping rule, and how it decided (see [Fit diagnostics](calibration_diagnostics.qmd#when-each-method-has-converged)) |
| `fit.trials`, `fit.to_df()` | Every evaluation: the values tried, and the objective at each |
| `fit.samples` | With a posterior, the draws: one row each, with its chain and number |
| `fit.trajectories` | With `'pmcmc'` or `'abc-smc'` on a stochastic compartmental model, the run that goes with each draw, which `fit.project()` continues; None otherwise |
| `fit.diagnostics` | `divergences` (NUTS), `acceptance` (particle MCMC and ABC-SMC), `tolerance` and `generations` (ABC-SMC), and `band` (95% of the model's values over draws from a posterior, which `fit.plot()` draws) |
| `fit.study` | With Optuna, Optuna's study, for its plots |
| `fit.summarize()`, `fit.plot(residuals=)`, `fit.project(scenarios, n_runs=, restart=, **kwargs)` | The table with the fit before and after; the model against the data (and the residuals); runs of scenarios from the fit |
